messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 35

He is 30, a Middle Eastern man who works as a tax inspector, and when he first speaks about the accident he does so the way he says he handles audits—carefully, fact by fact, as if precision might keep the worst parts contained. Before the crash, he describes himself as methodical, proud of being dependable. He likes work that requires order. He spends his days reviewing records, checking figures, noticing discrepancies other people miss. He says he used to believe that if he paid attention, if he followed rules, most problems could be prevented.

The collision happens on an ordinary weekday evening. He is driving home after a long day visiting businesses, tired but alert, thinking about whether he has enough time to stop for groceries before heading back to his apartment. At an intersection, another car comes through at high speed and slams into the driver’s side of his vehicle. He remembers the violence of the impact more than a sequence: the explosion of glass, metal folding inward, the sound in his ears afterward like static. For a few seconds he thinks, with total certainty, that he is about to die. He cannot move right away. He smells gasoline and something hot, and his mind fixes on the possibility that the car will catch fire before anyone reaches him. He tries to pull air into his lungs, but his chest feels pinned. Later he learns that bystanders call emergency services and that he is extracted alive with no catastrophic injuries, but what stays with him is the trapped feeling and the belief, in those moments, that his life is ending on the side of the road.

In the weeks after, family and colleagues tell him he is lucky. He repeats that word himself—lucky—without feeling it. His bruises fade faster than his fear. He startles at screeching brakes outside his apartment. At night he jerks awake with the impact replaying in his body before he is fully conscious. Sometimes he sees the oncoming headlights just as he is falling asleep and sits upright in bed, heart pounding, soaked in sweat. He begins sleeping with the television on because silence makes room for the memory. In the morning he feels ashamed of how exhausted he is from simply trying to rest.

He goes back to work sooner than he feels ready because routine seems safer than being alone with his thoughts. But driving to inspections becomes its own ordeal. He grips the steering wheel so hard his hands cramp. At intersections he scans every direction repeatedly, unable to trust green lights or other drivers’ intentions. If a car approaches too fast from the side, his whole body tightens and he brakes reflexively, even when there is no danger. He starts leaving excessively early so he can take longer routes that avoid busy roads. When possible, he rearranges visits to businesses close to the office and tells coworkers he is streamlining his schedule. What was once ordinary travel now consumes his energy before the workday has even started.

At the office, his concentration is not what it was. He reads the same line of a financial statement several times and realizes he has not absorbed it. A slammed file drawer or a shout from the hallway sends a shock through him. He covers by working later, checking his calculations again and again, unwilling to let anyone see mistakes. This only leaves him more depleted. He says he used to enjoy the satisfying clarity of finding inconsistencies in documents; now his mind keeps slipping back to the crushed door, the smell of gasoline, the helpless waiting.

His marriage, already strained before the crash, unravels in the months that follow. He becomes withdrawn and irritable in ways he does not recognize in himself. His former wife asks simple questions—How was your day? Are you coming to dinner at my parents’?—and he hears them as demands he cannot meet. He avoids gatherings because crowded rooms feel noisy and unpredictable, and because he is tired of people asking if he is “back to normal.” When she reaches for him at night, he sometimes flinches before he can stop himself. He hates the look on her face when that happens. They argue about his distance, his temper, his refusal to talk, and eventually the marriage ends. He speaks of the divorce with a flatness that gives way, at times, to quiet guilt. He wonders whether the accident took more from him than he admitted.

Now, even months later, his world still feels subtly organized around threat. He sits facing exits in cafés. He notices speeding cars before he notices the weather. He keeps replaying alternate versions of the crash—if he had left work ten minutes later, if he had taken another road, if he had seen the car sooner. Part of him knows these thoughts change nothing, but he cannot stop searching them for a sense of control. He says he feels older than 30, as if his nervous system no longer believes in ordinary life. And yet he continues to show up to work in pressed shirts, carrying neat folders, trying to inhabit the reliable man he was before that evening at the intersection, while privately bracing for impact that never quite feels over.
